Partition the reference by state, and run the cascade over the partition

Source: R/partition.R
pf_partition.Rd

A shard's peak memory tracks the size of the reference it holds, and nothing else moved it — not thread count, not batch size, not collecting between passes, not collapsing duplicate reference rows (dev/MEMORY-FINDINGS.md). Slicing the reference is therefore the only measured route to running more than one shard at a time: the largest state slice peaks at 5.24 GB against 37 GB for the whole reference, so eleven fit in 68 GB where one did before (dev/STATE-PARTITION-FINDINGS.md).

Queries must be routed on the normalized state, not on the raw recorded one. The two disagree on only 2 of 74,673 identities, so this is not where the recall goes — but 770 carry no normalized state at all, and those match nothing under a state-blocked pass by construction. They are routed to "_NONE" and reach the reference only through the cross-state phase, which is exactly the set of passes that could ever have matched them.

Phase 1 runs the state-local passes inside each shard. Phase 2 runs the cross-state passes against the whole reference, on the queries no shard resolved. The candidate sets are then unioned and selected and tiered once — which is what np_cascade() does internally, and the reason a query's runner-up margin is still computed across all of its candidates.

Usage

pf_partition_reference(
  ref,
  states = NULL,
  min_rows = 5000L,
  token_cols = c("name_key", "name_acro"),
  verbose = TRUE
)

pf_route_queries(query, shards)

pf_run_partitioned(
  grants,
  part,
  ref,
  config = npmatch::np_config(),
  method = "hier",
  passes = c(pf_staged_passes("lean", concat = TRUE), pf_recovery_passes(state = TRUE)),
  verbose = TRUE
)

Arguments

ref

The unpartitioned bundle, for the cross-state phase.

states

Which states to build. Defaults to every state present.

min_rows

States with fewer rows than this are merged into a single "_SMALL" shard, so the territories do not each pay a process.

verbose

Per-shard progress.

query

A normalized np_query.

shards

Names of the available shards.

grants

A prepared frame from pf_prepare_grants().

part

A pf_partition_reference() result.

config, method

Passed to the cascade.

passes

Full pass list; split internally into state-local and cross-state.

Value

A list of bundles, one per shard, each holding a sliced reference and a hybrid ref_index. name_freq and token_idf are shared unchanged — they are consumed by scoring, which must see the whole corpus.

A character vector of shard labels, one per query row.

A pf_match, the same class the monolithic path returns.

Why nine of eleven passes partition

Seven passes block on state outright, and A1-name-zip5 and D2-prefix block on ZIP5, which determines state. A query can only reach a reference row in its own state under any of them, so holding the other 89% of the reference buys nothing. The two that genuinely cross state lines — C1-name-any and C2-dba-any — are also the cheapest in the cascade, 6,284 and 176 candidates against B2-token-concat's 71,105.

The two things that make a slice behave like the whole

Corpus statistics. np_block() gates tokens on document frequency and IDF, both derived from the reference. Rebuilt on a slice they describe California rather than the country, and a token common nationally but rare in-state stops being gated — on the first attempt that produced more candidate pairs from a tenth of the reference. pf_partition_reference() therefore builds a hybrid index: rows positional within the slice, because ref_index$base$row indexes the frame it was built from, and df_base, df_concat and n_reference taken from the whole corpus.

Order of passes. np_cascade() withholds queries that an earlier pass resolved to YES, so a query's candidate set depends on how far it travelled. Running the state-local passes first and the cross-state passes on what remains changes what is pending when C1/C2 run, relative to the monolithic order where they sit between B2 and D1. That is a real difference and it is why pf_run_partitioned() is validated on tier agreement rather than assumed identical.
